General.Description:
The Marathon des Sables covers two hundred and fifty kilometres across the Moroccan Sahara in six stages over seven days, in temperatures that regularly exceed fifty degrees Celsius. Competitors carry their own food and equipment. Organisers provide water and very little else. Approximately ninety percent of entrants finish. The other ten percent have stories worth telling.

Omar Al-Rashid entered the Marathon des Sables the year after his brother died of cancer. He had run recreationally for six years. He had never run further than a half-marathon. He finished the race in four days, nineteen hours, and forty-three minutes — placing in the top quarter of the field.

Desert Run is not principally about running. It is about the decision to do something extreme as a response to grief, and about what you discover when you strip away everything that constitutes your ordinary life and replace it with sand, heat, and the singular objective of keeping moving forward. Al-Rashid writes with the controlled precision of a man who has had a long time to think about what the desert taught him.

Fierce, beautiful, and quietly transformative.
